description: Solaris Core is an independent software and science project from Costa Rica, led by Roney Rigg Mora. We build free and open-source tools for planetary science and education, including the Lunar Site Navigator for this challenge. This is a solo team and we are not looking for new members at this time.
summary: The Lunar Site Navigator is a free, open-source web tool that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates near the Moon's south pole. Near the pole the Sun barely rises, so choosing where and when to land is hard. For any chosen site and date, the tool shows whether there is Sun for power and a line of sight to Earth, when that changes, and when the next window with both opens. It uses NASA's LOLA terrain data and SPICE ephemerides, and it runs in the browser as a single offline file, in English and Spanish. Our main site, 456, is not the brightest of the 10 candidates analyzed, but the most robust. We state the model's limits openly.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The Lunar Site Navigator helps mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates near the Moon's south pole. For a chosen site and date it shows whether there is Sun for power and line of sight to Earth, when that changes, and when the next window with both opens.

HOW IT WORKS

It runs in the browser as a single offline file, in English and Spanish. Sun and Earth positions come from SPICE (DE440 ephemerides), computed hourly from 2026-11-01 to 2045-10-31. Visibility is traced over LOLA terrain toward 360 azimuths out to 200 km, with lunar curvature and no atmospheric refraction.

FEATURES

Side-by-side comparison of up to 3 sites, the same site on two dates, a window calendar for missions of 1 to 28 days, a delay planner, a "move the lander 100 m" sensitivity map, custom coordinates, horizon panoramas, a play button through time, a share link and CSV export.

RESULT AND CREATIVITY

Our main site is 456: not the brightest of the 10 candidates we analyzed, but the most robust. Site 14 gets more light, but its landing pocket is small and fragile. We chose robustness over brightness as a deliberate criterion.

LIMITS, STATED OPENLY

The model overestimates light by about 7 points at the candidates compared with LROC imagery, Earth visibility has no imagery validation, and the ranking is our own provisional judgment, not a NASA selection.

TOOLS AND SI ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

Built as a single-file web app (JavaScript) and hosted on Cloudflare Workers. Source code (MIT license): https://github.com/rodneymora94965/lunar-site-navigator

Super Intelligence (SI) tools assisted with code, tests, documentation, translation and the illustrative 3D renders. The renders carry a visible "Illustrative render · AI-assisted" label and contain invented details (the lander, rocks, stars and Earth's continents). The terrain and ephemeris data are NASA's and were not generated by SI. The idea, the question, the data choices and the site-selection criterion are the author's.

Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
